title: Weak orders and slow collections kept Turkish firms cautious even as borrowing rates eased
bank: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
summary: Interviews during July–September found little evidence that easier borrowing costs were translating into an investment recovery. Turkish firms described weak domestic sales, fewer export orders, falling production and longer waits to collect invoices. Lower input costs and deferred capital spending reduced the amount some firms needed to borrow. At the same time, slower payments made cash management harder. A reduction in reported financing needs could therefore coexist with worsening credit conditions for individual suppliers (Box 2.3, pp. 1–3).

Sales softened most clearly in July and recovered slightly from August. Back-to-school and post-summer demand disappointed firms’ earlier expectations. Households delayed expensive purchases until the promotional season, leaving durable goods weaker than non-durables and semi-durables. In Chart 1 the balance is the share of interviewed firms reporting stronger demand perceptions less the share reporting weaker ones. Perceptions encompass sales, orders and expectations. A recovery in that balance indicates a change in how widespread improvement is. It gives no estimate of sales growth. Initial October interviews suggested that recent capital-market developments added little further pressure on demand. Firms still expected promotions to bring some deferred purchases forward, although squeezed margins limited their ability to discount.

The foreign order book provided little insulation. Earlier freight disruption had temporarily favoured Turkish suppliers able to deliver to Europe more quickly. That benefit faded, while European investment outside energy and defence weakened. Demand from the US, a recovery in the Middle East and efforts to reach African markets provided partial offsets. Tourism reached seasonal volumes, helped by last-minute bookings and discounts. The distinction between volume and margin matters for exporters and tourist operators alike.

Companies reported some interest-rate relief after weekly repo auctions resumed. Access to finance remained difficult and delayed collections made firms more selective about customers, further restraining business-to-business trade. Firms with strong equity could continue selected capacity investments. More generally they preferred automation, modernisation or projects delivering rapid cost savings. Most planned to maintain employment over the following six months, partly because earlier cuts and the difficulty of finding skilled staff limited further reductions. Slower input and energy cost increases, competition and weak demand constrained selling prices. Renewed September geopolitical risk threatened to reverse some of that cost relief.

The separate discussion of proposed EU production requirements adds a longer horizon. Chart 2 describes the composition of EU manufacturing value added. Chart 3 measures the EU share in Turkish exports in selected sectors. They describe industrial scale and market dependence, while the direct commercial risk depends on actual procurement eligibility and origin or low-carbon rules. Automotive companies discussed alternative European assembly sites, local partners and acquisitions. Suppliers feared losing future projects if an anchor manufacturer relocated. Interviewees also pointed to the cost to European producers of disrupting integrated supply chains and the potential benefit if barriers were reduced. The report records contingency planning. It supplies no confirmed relocation or quantified investment loss (pp. 3–4).

questions.question: Would year-end promotions recover deferred sales at a sustainable margin?
questions.detail: The interviews point to postponed purchases and pressure to generate cash. Compare unit sales, realised selling prices, inventories and retailer gross margins through the promotion period. A volume rebound financed by larger discounts has a different earnings implication from a recovery in willingness to pay.

questions.question: Which suppliers were financing customers for longer?
questions.detail: Firms describe slower collections even as some borrowing rates eased. Receivable ageing, trade-credit terms and bank credit by industry would show where liquidity needs were building, and whether suppliers facing long delays were also losing access to funding.

questions.question: Which existing order books would the proposed European rules actually affect?
questions.detail: The report identifies automotive and other supply chains, while the legal scope and Türkiye’s treatment remained uncertain. Compare the proposal’s eligibility provisions with the share of each supplier’s contracted revenue from publicly supported projects before valuing relocation risk.
